own_scenes.family: Soul y proto-funk: Stax, Nueva Orleans, Motown
own_scenes.desc: Tras la Bomba de James Brown, el soul dio un giro radical: el acento en el primer tiempo se oyó en «Superstition» de Stevie Wonder, «Inner City Blues» de Marvin Gaye y «Cloud Nine» de los Temptations; lo que empezó como un efecto se volvió norma, y el jam funk pasó a ser imprescindible para que un artista negro llegara a la gente en los setenta. Marvin Gaye preguntó «What’s Goin’ On».

notes.chapter: Cap. 8: The Family Stoned: I Wanna Take You Higher
notes.text: Motown aprovechó enseguida la fórmula de «Dance to the Music» con «Cloud Nine» de los Temptations (1968). Kool & the Gang, Earth, Wind & Fire y War siguieron los arreglos de Sly, con guitarras más ligeras y más teclados que James Brown; Herbie Hancock le dedicó un tema en Head Hunters. Chaka Khan, Patti LaBelle o Minnie Riperton ganaron control creativo, pero pocas instrumentistas siguieron el camino de la Family Stone: el funk fue un movimiento liderado por hombres negros.

What’s Going On (1971) de Marvin Gaye, nacido de la muerte de Tammi Terrell y de las historias de Vietnam de su hermano, fue rechazado por Gordy («el peor disco que he oído») y llegó al número 1 de soul: el primer gran disco concebido como un todo, que abrió la radio al realismo del funk. Le siguieron «Papa Was a Rollin’ Stone», «Back Stabbers» de los O’Jays o «(For God’s Sake) Give More Power to the People» de los Chi-Lites: lo que Nelson George llamó «canciones de redención en la era de las corporaciones». Gaye pasó luego al erotismo de Let’s Get It On (1973) y volvió con «Sexual Healing» antes de que su padre lo matara en 1984. Stevie Wonder, al cumplir veintiún años, ganó el control de su obra y con el Moog de Malcolm Cecil y Robert Margouleff grabó Talking Book, Innervisions, Fulfillingness’ First Finale y Songs in the Key of Life: soul con el ritmo de James Brown, el clavinet como base del funk (tras «Outa-Space» de Billy Preston) y «Living for the City», muy sampleado. Otros soul funky con mensaje: los Stylistics, Bloodstone, Main Ingredient, los Staple Singers, Al Green, Donny Hathaway. Funk es, en el fondo, soul duro con la banda a pleno rendimiento; el cantante de soul sin banda acabó en el disco.

influences.name: James Brown, el Padrino del Soul

refs.q: Soul music took a radical turn down south
refs.para: The James Brown Bomb was an explosion of such atomic proportions that its echoes can still be heard lingering today, just like the electromagnetic remnants of the Big Bang. Soul music took a radical turn down south, as the one-count could be heard on songs like Stevie Wonder’s “Superstition,” Marvin Gaye’s “Inner City Blues,” and the Temptations’ “Cloud Nine.” What began as an effect became a standard, as the funk jam became an essential aspect of any black artist’s ability to reach the people in the 1970s.
refs.chapter: Cap. 1: Introducción al funk: The Bomb

refs.q: Sly was the first to incorporate women into his self-contained musical unit as performers.
refs.para: Sly was the first to incorporate women into his self-contained musical unit as performers. His band was unique in this respect, and while the musical themes of equality were followed zealously by other artists, few developed such strong professional relationships with women. Lead singers in funky music bands like Chaka Khan and Rufus, Patti LaBelle, and Minnie Riperton developed a great degree of creative control of their music in the 1970s, but too few female instrumentalists found their way through the door. For all of its universality and freedom, funk and the era of black bands were still a movement led by black men.
refs.chapter: Cap. 8: The Family Stoned: I Wanna Take You Higher

refs.q: Marvin Gaye was a troubled man.
refs.para: Marvin Gaye was a troubled man. One of many frustrated pop crooners on the Motown label, he released dimensions within himself that his followers are still just beginning to comprehend. The death of his sparkling duet partner Tammi Terrell in March 1970 devastated him, along with constant problems with drugs, his father, and Motown brass. After a period of mourning, depression, and creation, Gaye produced a masterpiece of mood, melody, and bitter reality. This was the most important work of Gaye’s life, and the beginning of a new era for Motown. Gaye described the genesis of What’s Goin’ On to writer David Ritz in Divided Soul:

refs.q: What’s Goin’ On opened the door for the graphic realism of The Funk to get on the radio.
refs.para: The record sleeve featured lengthy liner notes penned by Gaye himself, as well as a “family photo album” collage. Gaye had single-handedly redefined the structure of black popular music from a singles format to an album format, and opened up the parameters of personal exploration and revelation on a popular record. Almost overnight the sound of young America had matured, and reality became more important than fluffy feel-good sounds. What’s Goin’ On opened the door for the graphic realism of The Funk to get on the radio.

refs.q: It was one man, actually, who brought together the entire black American musical tradition for the world to witness in the 1970s.
refs.para: It was one man, actually, who brought together the entire black American musical tradition for the world to witness in the 1970s. Stevie Wonder (born Steveland Morris in Saginaw, Michigan, on May 13, 1950) had been waiting for his twenty-first birthday, at which point he could write his own contract and therefore produce his own music. He rewrote musical history on his own terms from that point on.

refs.q: Funk is essentially hard-core soul music, with the band in soulful, full effect along with the singers.
refs.para: One clear distinction between the sound of a strong soul singer and that of a funk band was the strength of the band driving the songs. A good example of this is Chaka Khan’s solo work in the late seventies (standard soul singing), compared to her work with Rufus, a jam-packed band in which she collaborated, cowrote, and covered her fullest range playing The Funk. A similar thing happened with Lionel Richie. The superstar pop balladeer of the 1980s performed a greater range of styles as lead singer of the Commodores in the 1970s, including dirty swamp-dog funk. This is why there is very little conflict between the notions of funk and soul. Funk is essentially hard-core soul music, with the band in soulful, full effect along with the singers. The high standards of sixties soul had elevated The Funk into a complete genre of music—United Funk—with soul vocals and funk grooves. With the intrusion of artificial means of music making, the soul singer without a strong band inevitably wound up playing disco.

own_scenes.family: Soul y proto-funk: Stax, Nueva Orleans, Motown
own_scenes.desc: El imperio de Berry Gordy fue un fenómeno de capitalismo negro, pero en los setenta solo sobrevivieron los artistas que escribían su material (Stevie Wonder, Marvin Gaye, Smokey Robinson, Michael Jackson). Norman Whitfield, que pasó de chupatintas a productor, le dio un filo más áspero («I Heard It Through the Grapevine» de Gladys Knight) y, mientras Sly arrasaba en 1968, cambió el sonido de los Temptations: temas largos con guitarras rockeras, efectos espaciales, drogas («Cloud Nine», «Psychedelic Shack», «Ball of Confusion») y orgullo negro, ropa a lo Hendrix y, al final, «Papa Was a Rollin’ Stone» (1972), soul con mensaje. La huella de P-Funk era clara (Eddie Hazel y Billy Nelson tocan en «Shakey Ground»); Whitfield convirtió a los Undisputed Truth en una banda de black rock pintada de plata. Los músicos de sesión, los Funk Brothers, trabajaban en la sombra: el bajista James Jamerson, que sacaba líneas de cómo hablaba o caminaba la gente, influyó a todos. Cuando Motown se mudó a Los Ángeles, la banda se quedó en Detroit y la magia se perdió.

refs.q: One in-house writer named Norman Whitfield took some chances with the Motown formula that paid off huge funk dividends
refs.para: One in-house writer named Norman Whitfield took some chances with the Motown formula that paid off huge funk dividends for Motown records, particularly with the Temptations. Working his way up from paper pusher to producer at the label, Norman Whitfield injected a rougher edge into Motown’s hit machine, an edge that can be heard on the Temptations’ “Ain’t Too Proud to Beg,” “Can’t Get Next to You,” and clearly on Gladys Knight’s rendition of “I Heard It Through the Grapevine.” In 1968, as Sly and the Family Stone was scorching the charts, Whitfield completely changed the Temptations’ sound and recorded wild, extended songs and topical themes such as “Psychedelic Shack,” “Ball of Confusion,” and “Cloud Nine.” There were rock-style guitars, spacey sound effects, and references to psychedelic drugs. The George Clinton, Sly Stone, and Jimi Hendrix influences were obvious, as was the drug-oriented subject matter. Temptations’ lead singer Eddie Kendricks can be heard on “Take a Stroll Through Your Mind” singing “one drag was all it took/and I was hooked.” The chorus to the Temptations’ No. 2 pop hit “Cloud Nine” went, “I’m doing fine/on cloud nine.” Perhaps even more significant was the strident black pride themes, heard on tunes like “Message from a Black Man,” and “Slave.”

refs.q: Bassist James Jamerson was the best-known musician and had perhaps the strongest impact of any single player in the Motown family.
refs.para: Bassist James Jamerson was the best-known musician and had perhaps the strongest impact of any single player in the Motown family. His ability to cook a groove, skipping, stopping, and swinging while still hanging tight (listen to Stevie Wonder’s “For Once in My Life” or “Uptight”), influenced musicians everywhere, and made it difficult for live acts to replicate his sound.
